message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may:
 • Withhold rent (but only after giving written notice and following the proper procedure).
 • Make the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent (after giving notice).
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment, excessive noise, or unlawful entry. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** (unless it’s an emergency).
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or to show the unit to prospective tenants/buyers. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Privacy** | • The landlord cannot enter your unit without notice (except emergencies). | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek a court order. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends automatically unless renewed. | • Provide written notice in the manner specified in the lease. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
 • Unpaid rent
 • Damage beyond normal wear & tear
 • Cleaning costs if the unit isn’t left in a reasonable condition | • Review the itemized statement. If you disagree, negotiate or file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent (after giving notice). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to the notice, attend the hearing, and present evidence (e.g., proof of payment). | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Rent can increase at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days). | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • If utilities are not clearly assigned, you can negotiate or seek clarification. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent. | • Obtain written permission; otherwise, you may be liable for the lease. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Purchase a policy covering personal property and liability. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Note dates, notice periods, and responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, and written communication. 3. **Keep Copies of All Notices** – Written notices from the landlord and your responses. 4. **Know the Local Code Enforcement Agency** – Many cities have housing departments that can help with complaints. 5. **Seek Legal Advice if Needed** – A tenant‑rights organization or attorney can help if you face eviction or disputes. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | Link | |----------|----------------|------| | Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) | Information on landlord‑tenant laws, complaint filing | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ | | Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) | Fair housing complaints | https://www.tchr.texas.gov/ | | Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection | Guidance on lease disputes | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/ | | Texas Small Claims Court | Filing claims up to $20,000 | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | | Local Housing Authority | City‑specific ordinances and assistance | Search your city’s official website | --- #### When to Call a Lawyer - **Unresolved Eviction Notice** – If you believe the eviction is unlawful. - **Large Security Deposit Dispute** – If the landlord refuses to return the deposit or disputes deductions. - **Discrimination Complaint** – If you suspect unlawful discrimination. - **Major Habitability Issues** – If the landlord refuses to repair critical problems. --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely notice for landlord entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for ending your tenancy. Keep records, communicate in writing, and know where to seek help if your rights are violated.
